Astronomy and observing the sky:
Astronomy is the science that studies objects in space, such as stars, planets, moons and galaxies. People observe the sky with the naked eye, with optical telescopes (refracting telescopes use lenses, reflecting telescopes use mirrors), with radio telescopes, and with telescopes in space.

Light travels at about 300,000 km/s. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10^12 km. Astronomy is a science based on evidence. Astrology is not, because its claims cannot be tested.

Many Iranian scientists, such as Al-Sufi, Omar Khayyam and Nasir al-Din Tusi, made important contributions to astronomy.
Galaxies and distances in space:
A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity. Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars and a diameter of about 100,000 light-years. Galaxies are spiral, elliptical or irregular.

Distances in space are too large for kilometres, so astronomers use the astronomical unit (AU, the Earth-Sun distance, about 1.5 × 10^8 km) and the light-year. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away. The Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away.

Because light takes time to travel, looking far away means looking into the past.
Constellations and finding directions:
A constellation is a pattern of stars that people have named. There are 88 official constellations. The stars in a pattern are usually not close to each other in space.

Earth rotates from west to east once in 24 hours, about 15 degrees each hour. So the Sun and stars seem to rise in the east and set in the west. In the northern hemisphere, stars seem to circle around Polaris, the North Star, which is almost directly above the North Pole.

The angle of Polaris above the horizon equals the observer's latitude. The Big Dipper's two pointer stars lead to Polaris. A compass or a shadow stick can also find directions.
The solar system and its planets:
The solar system is the Sun and all the objects that orbit it. The Sun holds more than 99% of the mass. There are eight planets. The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and rocky. The four outer planets are the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and the ice giants Uranus and Neptune.

The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Pluto is a dwarf planet. A planet orbits the Sun, is nearly round, and has cleared its orbit of other large objects.

The Earth-Sun distance is 1 AU. Neptune is about 30 AU away. Venus is the hottest planet, about 465 °C, because of its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere.
Moons, asteroids and space travel:
A moon is a natural satellite that orbits a planet. Earth's Moon orbits in about 27.3 days and shows phases over about 29.5 days. Mercury and Venus have no moons. Asteroids are rocky bodies, mostly in the asteroid belt. Comets are balls of ice and dust. A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.

A rocket must reach the escape velocity of 11.2 km/s to leave Earth. The first satellite, Sputnik 1, launched in 1957. Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space in 1961. Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon in 1969. The International Space Station orbits at about 400 km altitude at about 7.7 km/s. Iran launched its first satellite, Omid, in 2009.
